articles.title: Exchange rate’s woeful tale
articles.content: THE preoccupation of exchange rate fundamentalists in Pakistan with a single, partial indicator — Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) — is astonishing. As Nadeem ul Haque argued in an illuminating article, fixing or deliberately boosting exchange rates effectively ended with Bretton Woods’ collapse in the 1970s. Research has since confirmed that the exchange rate is a market price — the price of one currency in terms of another, determined by underlying economic conditions — and not a policy tool. Hence, the exchange rate is an endogenous variable reflecting domestic inflation, productivity, external balances, capital flows, reserve adequacy, fiscal credibility, interest-rate differentials, and market expectations. As Haque notes, “The rupee does not weaken because someone decides to weaken it. It weakens because underlying conditions make the existing price unsustainable.” REER has a legitimate but limited purpose. It measures changes in the nominal exchange rate adjusted for relative price movements against trading partners. But an index reading of 100, based on a selected base year, doesn’t establish an optimal exchange rate. Nor does a deviation from 100 automatically signal overvaluation or undervaluation. REER says little about balance-of-payments sustainability, foreign exchange availability from non-trade sources or exporters’ ability to compete through quality, technology, productivity, and delivery. There are questions to address before treating REER as an authoritative guide to exchange rate policy. First, does the base year 2010 represent an equilibrium exchange rate? Pakistan recorded acurrent account deficit of $3.95 billion,around two per cent of GDP, that year, compared with a near-balanced account in 2026. Second, have trade weights and trading partner composition remained representative over 16 years, especially after the China FTA? Third, have movements in individual partners’ currencies been adequately reflected in an index referencing the US dollar? Fourth, the choice of price deflator (CPI, PPI, unit labour costs or GDP deflator) can produce very different results. These points need serious thought before prescriptions are based on a single index. REER doesn’t capture many of the external account components. Workers’ remittances have grown faster than merchandise exports. They’re a major source of foreign exchange, financing imports of raw material, equipment and fuel, enabling domestic industry to use productive capacity that would otherwise be underemployed. They help build reserves, boost external stability, and reduce reliance on borrowing. FDI, portfolio investment, and external debt disbursements provide more foreign exchange liquidity. Assessments limited to REER overlook these determinants of external sustainability. Questions must be addressed before treating REER as an authoritative guide to exchange rate policy. Three empirical tests help establish whether the exchange rate is artificially managed or broadly market-determined. The first is the differential between official interbank and open-market rates. It peaked at Rs10-15 per dollar in FY2023. As reserves accumulated and market conditions normalised, the gap narrowed to its customary Rs0.50-2 range, indicating a more unified foreign exchange market. The second test is whether administrative restrictions on imports and profit and dividend repatriation are being used to suppress foreign exchange demand. Such curbs were imposed in FY2023 when SBP reserves fell to $3bn or so. Imports declined to $53bn and profit and dividend repatriation to just $331 million against normal levels of about $70bn and $2bn. Last fiscal, imports recovered to $71bn. Profit and dividend remittances reached $2.3bn. Arrears were cleared and current obligations met. This restoration hardly supports the view that the exchange rate is being sustained through administrative demand suppression. The third, perhaps most compelling, test is whether SBP has depleted its reserves to defend a parity. In FY2023, reserves fell to about $3bn recovering to around $21bn despite annual external debt-servicing dues of about $25bn. This accumulation occurred while the rate was around Rs280 per dollar and REER above 100. It’s difficult to reconcile this outcome with the claim that an artificial exchange rate is being maintained when SBP is mopping up surplus dollar liquidity after interbank clearance. Historical comparisons reinforce this view. Between 2015 and 2018, the rupee was maintained around Rs104 per dollar, but SBP reserves declined from $18bn to $9bn. In contrast, in 2000-2007 when reserves increased from barely $1bn to $13bn, the exchange rate remained stable around Rs60 and exports more than doubled from $9bn to $19bn. Still, critics said the rate was artificially defended, overlooking the net foreign exchange inflows being sterilised to prevent excessive appreciation and protect exporters’ competitiveness. Market expectations are another important aspect. In Pakistan, they are often driven by a bandwagon effect instead of rational assessments of fundamentals. When reserves fall below comfortable levels, depreciation expectations can become self-fulfilling. Exporters withhold dollar proceeds within the permitted 90-day surrender period, anticipating a better rate; importers advance foreign exchange requirements to avoid future depreciation. Supply contracts and demand rises putting pressure on the rupee. The anticipated depreciation then materialises. Would a 10pc depreciation advocated by REER fundamentalists improve competitiveness? Foreign buyers may demand price discounts of at least 5pc from exporters, treating additional rupee earnings as a windfall. About 40pc of exports use imported inputs including fuel, LNG, and textile raw materials. Their costs rise, leaving exporters with a net gain of perhaps only 2-3pc. The impact goes beyond exporters. Costlier imports fuel inflation, hurting poorer households whose main asset is their labour and whose wages, particularly in an informal economy with extensive underemployment, do not adjust proportionately. The central bank may raise interest rates, increasing domestic borrowing costs. Imported machinery becomes costlier, forcing investors to put off or abandon projects, hurting both investment and growth. As the rupee cost of servicing external debt increases, partly offset by higher import-duty collections, government may have to borrow more, crowding out private-sector credit. Foreign investors earn lower dollar returns, discouraging fresh investment. The lesson is that exchange-rate stability can’t be engineered through administrative intervention or depreciation alone. It must rest on credible fiscal management, a broader tax base, sound trade and tariff policies, remunerative energy pricing, higher productivity and prudent monetary management. Together, these policies reduce the need for disruptive exchange-rate adjustments. Pakistan must not treat REER as a magic number and depreciation as a remedy. The aim should not be an arbitrary index reading but sustainable external competitiveness, stronger reserves, higher exports and investment, and protection of purchasing power. The exchange rate is a reflection of economic fundamentals, not a substitute for them. Correcting symptoms while neglecting underlying weaknesses will only perpetuate the rupee’s woeful tale. The writer is a former State Bank governor.
articles.author: Ishrat Husain

articles.title: When home is hell
articles.content: ON an ordinary March afternoon this year, the children of a household in Lahore’s Choong district gathered for their uncle’s small promise of treats. Among them was four-year-old Azan, who was led out for a stroll by his uncle. It all ended eight hours later in the isolated outskirts of Quaid-i-Azam Industrial Estate — with Azan dead. The minor’s body, when recovered, showed a two-inch exposed spinal cord attaching the head and mutilated remains. Azan had reportedly been tortured and eventually killed with an eight-inch-long knife by his own father, allegedly in a calculated bid to implicate a third party. Azan is just one of several children who are killed every month by people known to them. Moving back, in October, a 13-year-old in Mianwali was shot dead by her cousin for not wearing a hijab. In September, a three-year-old in Islamabad was kidnapped, raped, and murdered by her brother-in-law. In August, an 18-month-old in Karachi died after being raped by her 17-year-old cousin, while in July, a six-year-old boy was beaten up, raped, and strangled with a wire by his neighbour, and a four-year-old girl in Gujranwala was set on fire by her mother on suspicion of being ‘possessed’. In May, a father in Vehari repeatedly raped his three daughters aged 14, 11, and nine for six consecutive months; while three children aged six, four, and three were killed and found hanging from the fans in their home in Multan. A month earlier, in April, a mother in Lahore brutally slit the throats of her three children, luring them through a sadistic ‘game’ of hide-and-seek. Occurring within the safe confines of the home, these tragedies shocked and enraged us more than others, but our protest ended in quiet resignation, as it did in 2022 when an eight-year-old was tortured and poisoned by her grandparents for failing at household chores, and in 2015 when a 12-year-old was beaten to death by her father for not making properly round rotis. Homes repeatedly turn into hell for children as our criminal justice system is unequipped to intercept and prevent attacks within the home. Statutes such as the ICT and Sindh Child Protection Acts create institutional bodies that address minors’ welfare, but they lack the authority to adopt anticipatory, prompt, and intrusive measures to ensure child safety. Our laws are reactive rather than anticipatory. Even the landmark Zainab Alert, Response, and Recovery Act, 2020, creates a protection mechanism for missing children that is enforceable only after the abduction is reported. As a result, attacks on children in public are not easily prevented. Our criminal justice system is unequipped to intercept and prevent attacks within the home. Recently, a five-year-old in Haripur was raped and left to die after being lured out of her home to see her father; an eight-year-old in Lahore was sexually harassed in a grocery store by the owner, and an eight-year-old in Sargodha was raped and murdered in a grocery store. Even when these victims were seen being accompanied or coaxed by a group of men or being eyed by strangers, the palpable threat of attack was ignored by those present at the scene. It was also in the presence of bystanders in Multan that 15-year-old Wasim was tortured and then run over by his employer recently. Whether it was their indifference or ignorance, they abandoned the weakest, most vulnerable members of society — our children. Being voiceless, defenceless and weak, children are considered dispensable. It is, therefore, easy to ignore injustices against them. We tolerate inadequate child protection laws and mechanisms, ignore the proliferation of pornographic content, disregard paedophilic customs such as trading minor boys, and permit appalling lectures advocating marriage with girls as young as four. Our complicity and apathy have normalised child abuse and allowed it to persist, putting Pakistan third on the global map for child abuse. Around 2,000 cases of child abuse were reported in just the first six months of the current year. Sahil reported over 3,600 in 2025. In 2024, 21 children were being abused daily. Reducing such horrifying figures demands enforceable protection under the law. Justice Jawad Hasan in 2023 (Zafar Khizer vs the Federation of Pakistan)initiated a shift in discourse from viewing children as ordinary citizens to viewing them as vulnerable citizens categorised as ‘child citizens’ and entitled to a higher degree of protection and concern under the law. Justice Usman G. Rashid last month said that the child citizen is entitled to fundamental rights in their independent capacity that cannot be displaced by any parental authority. While the concept of the child citizen as an independent rights holder is evolving through jurisprudence, it is insufficient without effective implementation and accountability. Mandatory reporting regimes should be introduced for designated professionals such as healthcare providers, instructors, and adults in child-related roles or positions of trust, as under Australian law and England’s Crime and Policing Act, 2026. Additional measures for prevention through reporting suspected child abuse and conducting child-sensitive investigations and follow-ups in such cases must be made compulsory in line with the spirit of Article 19 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. These obligations must be rooted not merely in law, but in a shared sense of humanity and a collective duty to protect the vulnerable because, as lawyer and human rights activist Asma Jahangir said, a society that fails to protect its children has, in fact, failed humanity’s most basic test.
articles.author: E.N. Bandial

articles.title: Enabling terrorism
articles.content: INSURGENCIES militarise society and spawn a conflict economy that empowers splinter insurgent groups with their own set of interests and objectives. These militant groups thrive in a governance vacuum as well as the ideological confusion in post-conflict societies. The TTP is amongst the classic examples of insurgency-begotten militancy and terrorism. Afghanistan is a quintessential case study of an insurgency-wracked nation that has given rise to other insurgencies and waves of terrorism. Afghanistan’s 10-year anti-Soviet insurgency achieved success but spawned another decade of internecine conflict that gave space to terrorist entities and subsequent international intervention against Al Qaeda terrorists operating from that country. Pakistan’s action against terrorist entities elicited an irate response from these violent groups in the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (now merged districts of KP), leading to a series of military operations from 2004 to 2017, driving the terrorists towards Afghanistan. After the US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021, the Taliban regime occupied Kabul and reneged on all its pledges made in the Doha Agreement and introduced a brutal, oppressive regime where there was no place for minorities, women, and non-Taliban Afghans. Soon after assuming power, the Taliban regime gave free rein to terrorist entities like the TTP and freed hardened criminals and terrorists from jails. After the US withdrawal, Pakistan extended an olive branch to the Taliban regime, offering humanitarian aid, trade facilities, and economic integration. But despite continual positive engagement, the Taliban did not abide by their counterterrorism commitments. Terrorist entities like TTP were given free rein to operate against Pakistan from secure sanctuaries in Afghanistan. When Pakistan started tightening its noose against these terrorists, their leadership was reportedly taken to Kabul’s Green Zone and hid amongst the civilian population. Insurgencies in Afghanistan have created an ecosystem of terror. At present, a blend of over 20 terrorist entities is operating under the benign gaze of the Taliban regime in Afghanistan. The Taliban are extremely adept at denialism and selling their anti-IS-K credentials. The reality is different, however, as terrorist entities like IS-K with a transnational agenda are operating under an entente cordiale between them and the Taliban regime. For many foreign powers, the Doha Agreement has been reduced to just two points — women’s rights and education — relegating inclusivity to the backburner due to the international community’s predilection for appeasing the Taliban. Pakistan is paying a huge price for this indulgence of the Taliban. After the US withdrawal, terrorist attacks in Pakistan surged manifold. Thousands have been killed and injured in terrorist attacks since. The two-faced Taliban have perfected the art of denying complicity in terrorism to curry favour with foreign donors. They are being facilitated in this endeavour by hostile foreign intelligence agencies that wish to keep the region destabilised for their geopolitical interests. The Taliban regime is thriving on an illicit economy where narco-trafficking, smuggling and extortion are being sponsored under official patronage, with the Taliban warlords having stakes in each criminal enterprise. The weapons left by Nato and US forces are being sold to terrorist entities. American and Nato forces, after the 2021 withdrawal, left behind weapons and equipment worth $7.12 billion, out of which large quantities were handed over or sold to terrorist entities like the TTP by the Taliban. Terrorist groups including the TTP and BLA have used these weapons against Pakistan under the patronage of the Taliban re-gime. According to the April 2025 report of the US Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction, the TTP accessed former Afghan army weapons, either transferred by Taliban authorities or acquired through the black market. Similar confirmation has been made by the UN Security Council Monitoring Team. By 2025, Pakistan’s security forces had recovered 293 US-made weapons and other gear from eliminated terrorists. Even a 2025 Washington Post investigation traced serial numbers of at least 63 weapons seized in Pakistan from terrorists to weapons supplied by the US to Afghan forces before 2021. Earlier insurgencies in Afghanistan birthed an ecosystem of terror, which is now being exported. The flow of arms to terrorist entities like the TTP and BLA from Afghanistan under the patronage of the Afghan Taliban regime is a taste of things to come for the entire international community, whose attention at present is consumed mostly by the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. The writer is a security analyst with a PhD degree from NUST.
articles.author: Dr Raashid Wali Janjua

articles.title: American change
articles.content: ON the Sunday beforeElection Dayin the US, the Democratic leadership was in uproar. The reason was Israel — though not obviously so. The action took place in Detroit, Michigan, where Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed was in a close race against Republican Mike Rogers. Rogers had run a campaign marked by Islamophobic attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, portraying him as a security threat and making unfounded allegations of extremist sympathies. In the primary election that decided the Democratic nominee, El-Sayed had defeated Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who had said she “dreamed of Israel” and had benefited from nearly $30 million in spending by pro-Israel lobbies. Despite this,El-Sayedwas able to win. Stevens decided that Sunday morning that she would endorse El-Sayed’s opponent, a man she had previously criticised. It was an extraordinary move that drew condemnation from her fellow Democrats and the American left. Appearing at an African-American church alongside Rogers, Stevens said that she just couldn’t support El-Sayed and would, instead, back the Republican. For the 48 hours until the election, Stevens got tons of attention. In an interview withCNN’sAnderson Cooper, she struggled to explain why she had withdrawn support for a candidate she had previously endorsed. Pro-Zionist commentators on the American right were gleeful. Maybe they hoped El-Sayed, who had openly opposed the war against Iran and called Gaza a genocide, would not win. It was a close election, and Stevens might persuade some Black and Jewish voters in Michigan not to vote for the man who would become the first Muslim senator in US history. As we know now, their predictions were wrong. El-Sayed defeated Rogers, becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Democrats also won control of both Houses of Congress, while several Muslim candidates, including Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib and Andre Carson won election or re-election. Democrat victories show voters oppose blanket support for Israel. Of all of them, El-Sayed had been the most plainspoken about the problem with US support for Israel. The particular mastery of his campaign was that it took the very Trumpian rhetoric of ‘America First’ and turned it on its head. El-Sayed argued that politicians who prioritised billions in aid to Israel over domestic needs were putting another country’s interests before those of ordinary Americans. This message resonated with voters all around the country. The issue of whether a politician is ‘America First’ rather than ‘Israel First’ has become part of the political conversation. This is particularly worrisome for establishment Democrats who would compete to demonstrate their love for Israel. The Democratic victories have clearly shown that the party voter wants to end the blanket support for Israel that has long been an American tradition. Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, presumptive leaders of the Senate and House, have both said that they do not support sending unending aid to Israel. They know which way the wind is blowing. The biggest evidence of this, however, came from the Republicans — really from the vice president himself. Even as the results were coming in, J.D. Vance took to X and wrote a lengthy post on why his party had lost so abysmally. Vance pointed directly to the war in Iran — which America entered at Israel’s behest — saying it had cost Republicans the election. It was a shocking yet understandable acknowledgment. It made sense for Vance — who is likely to run for president in 2028 — to try and distance himself from Trump right away. Now, he is seeking to ally himself with anti-Israel figures on the American right like Tucker Carlson. Carlson’s opposition to Israel is pointed in that he said he would have voted for El-Sayed simply because he was so fed up with unending support for Israel, which he thought had a harmful influence on America’s politics. Carlson has urged his supporters to understand how American democracy was being turned into a sham by Israeli influence. The America that woke up on Nov 4, 2026, is, therefore, a remarkably different America. Israel’s government has long relied on strong bipartisan support in Washington, and pro-Israel organisations have spent enormous sums to ensure that American politicians will always be in their pocket. Those days are not decisively over. It is likely that when the new lawmakers take office in January, legislation and limits will be pursued on all aid to Israel that could see the amount of military support drastically reduced. America voted for change this week but it is likely that it is Israel — with much reduced US support after January — that will see the greatest change in its circumstances. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.
articles.author: Rafia Zakaria

articles.title: The debt burden
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S external debt has nearlydoubledin a decade — from $68.7bn in 2015 to $135.1bn in 2025 — according to a new World Bank report. Public and publicly guaranteed debt accounts for $107.1bn of the total, private debt for $17.6bn, and short-term borrowing for $10.45bn. China is the largest single creditor with $22.4bn outstanding, followed by the World Bank and Asian Development Bank. The rise itself is not surprising but the pace is striking. Much of this borrowing went towards plugging external financing gaps, propping up reserves, and repaying older loans to keep the economy running. The debt spike describes an economy that invests, produces and earns too little to service what it owes. Debt has become the main constraint on our fiscal and economic prospects. Servicing debt eats up meagre financial resources, which should be expanding productive capacity for exports, and makes faster growth harder to reach. That leads to more borrowing. The government borrows to cover consumption, budget deficits, and external payments — not to build anything that pays for itself. Development spending is usually the first thing to be cut, and growth has crawled along at 2.7pc in recent years. There is nothing wrong with borrowing. Developing economies need foreign capital for infrastructure, energy, technology, and industry. The trouble starts when loans do not raise domestic productivity or lift exports. Successive governments have failed to tell apart borrowing that builds capacity from borrowing that only buys time. Pakistan’s recurring balance-of-payments crisis underscores this fact. The country’s exports are weak, the production base is narrow, investment is low, and fiscal deficits refuse to go away. So, the economy keeps relying on foreign and domestic loans. Remittances, rollovers by friendly countries, and one IMF programme after another may have staved off immediate default, but none of them has addressed the underlying problem. It does not matter much if the country can raise another loan or defer another repayment. What matters is whether the country can generate enough growth, tax revenue, and foreign exchange to meet its obligations without sacrificing its development. The situation calls for a credible, short- to long-term strategy to invest in projects that raise productivity, exports, and foreign exchange earnings. The strategy must be accompanied by wider reforms aimed at expansion of the tax base, more productive public spending, and lower costs of doing business. Exporters need energy that is reliable and competitively priced, policies they can predict, and access to modern technology. Without these, even fresh foreign investment and cheaper credit will yield little value, growth will remain anaemic, children stunted, and communities without basic services such as clean drinking water. And debt will continue to constrain the country’s economic sovereignty and prosperity.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Expendable LGs
articles.content: POLITICAL parties frequently appear reluctant to hold regular local bodies elections on one pretext or another. This attitude negates constitutional requirements for holding local government polls and establishing LGs, denying voters the right to elect their representatives at the grassroots level. As reported, the ECP has dropped plans to hold LG polls in KP due to the suspension of Article 140-A. After the proclamation of emergency in the province last month, the article had been suspended in specific districts. The centre has now suspended Article 140-A across the province, scuttling plans for LG polls in the foreseeable future. Questions have also been raised regarding the LG polls scheduled in Islamabad for Dec 20, as a petitioner has challenged delimitation in the high court. In Punjab, however, LG polls should be held in February 2027, unless new obstructions are created. It is unfortunate that both the state and political parties — which claim to be the flag-bearers of democracy — put in so much effort to keep third-tier governance in indefinite abeyance. Under the law, elections are supposed to take place 120 days after the term of an LG expires. However, in Pakistan, the law is routinely flouted. In KP, the LGs’ term expired in June, while in Punjab and Islamabad Capital Territory, LG polls should have been held in May 2022 and June 2021, respectively. A common tactic, particularly used by parties ruling a province, is to amend the LG laws so that delimitation and the electoral process are further postponed. This ploy ends up wasting taxpayers’ money and depriving citizens of their right to elect local representatives. To do away with the legal loopholes, it has been suggested that the Elections Act, 2017, be amended so that no changes to the LG law are allowed once an LG completes its term. Secondly, a constitutional amendment may be required to clarify the process of LG polls so that neither the centre nor the provinces can shirk this essential responsibility. Our cities, towns, and villages cannot develop without functioning and responsive LGs. Moreover, empowered local bodies also present a democratic alternative to the complicated question of forging new provinces, as they would, in theory, bring power and funds down to the local level.
articles.author: Editorial
